name: Finnish
intro: Finnish is a Uralic language, structurally distinct from the Scandinavian languages. Written standard and colloquial spoken Finnish differ substantially. Quantity contrasts in vowels and consonants carry meaning. Learn vowel harmony, consonant gradation and stem changes as part of words, rather than memorising a case ending without its stem.

foundation.name: Finnish
notes: Finnish uses the Latin alphabet with Å, Ä and Ö. Several letters occur mainly in loans and names. Length is meaningful: tuli = fire; tuuli = wind; tulli = customs. A doubled letter represents longer duration, not a second syllable by default.
Primary stress falls on the first syllable. y is a rounded front vowel /y/, ä is /æ/, ö is /ø/. Vowel harmony groups a/o/u against ä/ö/y; e/i are neutral. Suffixes often have back and front variants.

A dictionary form is not always the stem used before a suffix. Consonant gradation and other changes appear in inflection: kauppa → kaupassa. Learn a small paradigm rather than guessing from the final letter.
building: talo → talossa → talosta → taloon = house → in the house → out of the house → into the house. These suffixes are part of the word, not separate English prepositions.
talo + ssa → talossa; kylä + ssä → kylässä = in the village. Neutral vowels normally coexist with either group; compound parts can behave separately.
Luen kirjaa. = I am reading a book (ongoing/partial perspective). Luen kirjan. = I will read the book through / read the whole book. Object marking depends on more than definiteness.

sections.title: Sound, harmony and case stems
sections.explanation: Front/back vowel harmony affects many endings; e and i are neutral in the basic system. Long vowels and doubled consonants contrast with short ones. Case formation can change a noun's stem through gradation and other patterns: kauppa/kaupassa. Finnish has many cases, including local cases in series; their labels do not remove lexical government and metaphorical uses.
examples: in a house / out of a house / into a house
exercises: Why learn a noun with several forms?
The stem can change; endings alone do not predict every form.
What does vowel/consonant length practice require?
Meaningful audio contrasts and timed production, not just louder stress.

sections.title: Objects, partitive and boundedness
sections.explanation: Finnish object marking depends on negation, quantity and aspectual boundedness. A partitive object often presents an unbounded activity or incomplete quantity; a total object presents a bounded whole under appropriate conditions. Negated objects take partitive in core patterns. Form choice for total objects also depends on sentence construction, so it is not one uniform ending.
examples: Partitive frames the activity as unbounded.
Total object with a bounded reading interpretation.
exercises: Negate Luin kirjan.
En lukenut kirjaa. Negative auxiliary, past participle and partitive object.
Is partitive merely an indefinite article?
No. Quantity, negation and boundedness are central grammatical factors.

sections.title: Verb forms and the negative verb
sections.explanation: Finnish negative uses an inflecting negative auxiliary: en, et, ei, emme, ette, eivät. The main verb has a connegative or participial form according to tense. Present and past forms have person marking; perfect uses olla + participle. The conditional -isi- supports hypothetical reasoning and courtesy. Learn verb types with stem changes.
examples: First-person negative auxiliary plus connegative main verb.
exercises: Change En tiedä to we do not know.
Emme tiedä. The negative auxiliary carries person/number.
Why cannot English do not be translated as one fixed word?
The Finnish negative auxiliary inflects and interacts with tense and the main verb form.

sections.title: Participles, clauses and standard/spoken differences
sections.explanation: Participles and infinitival constructions compress clauses in formal prose. Relative joka inflects according to its role, with agreement and case patterns to learn. Standard Finnish minä olen and colloquial forms such as mä oon illustrate a wider gap than a minor accent difference. Keep a stable professional written standard while recognising conversational forms.
exercises: What should you track in a compressed clause?
Agent, time, case government, head noun and relationship to the main predicate.
Should colloquial forms automatically appear in formal reports?
No. Register must match audience and medium.

sections.title: Professional reading
sections.explanation:
Teaching passage: Tulokset osoittavat yhteyden kahden tekijän välillä. Ne eivät kuitenkaan todista, että toinen tekijä aiheuttaa toisen. Tutkimuksen olosuhteet on otettava huomioon johtopäätöstä arvioitaessa.
Translation: The results show a relationship between two factors. However, they do not prove that one causes the other. Study conditions must be considered when assessing the conclusion.
exercises: What is the role of eivät?
Third-person plural negative auxiliary agreeing with ne.
Summarise the passage in standard Finnish.
Preserve case relationships, causal caution and the distinction between formal and spoken forms.

rules.title: Personal pronouns
rules.explanation: Personal pronouns have distinct case forms. Verb endings often identify first/second person, allowing the pronoun to be omitted. Standard hän refers to a person without encoding male/female gender.

examples.translation: They called for an end to the fighting.
I'm in love with you already.
I am not a penguin.

rules.title: Present olla
rules.explanation: Olla agrees with the subject: olen, olet, on, olemme, olette, ovat. On is also used in many existential or possessive constructions whose syntax differs from a simple subject predicate.

examples.translation: When two people quarrel, a third rejoices.
Tom is grumpy.

examples.native: Tomin operoinut kirurgi on hyvin kokenut ja erittäin arvostettu.
examples.translation: The surgeon who did Tom's operation is very experienced and highly regarded.

rules.title: The negative verb
rules.explanation: Finnish negation conjugates the negative auxiliary for person and number. The ordinary lexical verb appears in a connegative form: en puhu, et puhu, ei puhu.

examples.native: Vannoin, että en puhuisi enää ikinä hänelle.
examples.translation: I vowed that I would never speak to her again.

examples.native: Miksi et ole vielä valmistanut illallista?
examples.translation: Why haven't you cooked dinner yet?

examples.native: En halua mennä naimisiin liian aikaisin.
examples.translation: I don't want to get married too early.

rules.title: Negative imperatives
rules.explanation: Älä gives a singular prohibition; älkää a plural/polite one. The following verb has an imperative-compatible form. These are not ordinary present negative auxiliary forms.

examples.native: Älä ikinä yritä tehdä tätä itse.
examples.translation: Don't ever try to do this by yourself.

examples.native: Älä unohda laittaa postimerkkejä kirjeisiin, jotka annoin sinulle postitettavaksi.
examples.translation: Please don't forget to put stamps on the letters I gave you to post.

examples.native: Älä juo olutta ennen vuoteeseen menoa.
examples.translation: Don't drink beer before going to bed!

rules.title: Past olla
rules.explanation: The past of olla agrees with the subject. It can be a main verb or a perfect/pluperfect auxiliary. Read any accompanying participle before choosing the analysis.

examples.translation: Mary is a big fan of theirs.
The room was packed.

examples.native: Kahdesti ja kolmasti olin sinua rakastanut, ennen kuin tunsin naamaasi tahi nimeäsi.
examples.translation: Twice and thrice had I loved thee before I knew thy face or name.

rules.title: Partitive nouns
rules.explanation: Partitive occurs in many quantities, negative objects and ongoing/unbounded object constructions. It is not merely the form for an indefinite English noun. Learn the case stem alongside the nominative.

examples.native: Käyn hakemassa vähän kahvia. Haluatko sinäkin?
examples.translation: I'm going to get myself some coffee. Do you want some?
How many books do you read a month?

examples.native: Mä luulen, että meillä on tarpeeksi rahaa.
examples.translation: I think we have enough money.

rules.title: Genitive singular
rules.explanation: Singular genitive often ends in -n with possible stem changes. It can express possession and participates in total-object marking in suitable constructions. The function depends on the sentence.

examples.translation: I want a picture of that dog.
Last Sunday I bought a new car.
Tom bought a new car.

rules.title: Inessive location
rules.explanation: Inessive -ssa/-ssä expresses many inside/location relations. Vowel harmony chooses the variant. Words such as missä contain the same case relation in an interrogative form.

examples.translation: Tom lived half his life in Boston.

examples.native: Tom vaikutti tuijottavan jotain huoneen nurkassa.
examples.translation: Tom seemed to be staring at something in the corner of the room.
I showered before breakfast.

rules.title: Elative source
rules.explanation: Elative -sta/-stä expresses movement out of, source and some governed complements. The noun stem may change before the ending. A word’s suffix must be checked against its actual paradigm.

examples.translation: Please don't tell anybody about this.
Tom envied Mary's success.
I like your friends.

rules.title: Allative destination
rules.explanation: Allative -lle commonly marks a destination onto/at a surface or a recipient. Pronouns have their own stems. English to can also map to other Finnish cases.

examples.translation: Tom lied to you.
Tell me about it!
All this is strange to me.

rules.title: Adessive and possession
rules.explanation: Adessive marks many surface/location meanings. A possessive construction often uses an adessive possessor plus olla: Minulla on kirja. The possessed noun is not automatically an accusative object.

examples.native: Minulla on ollut todella kova päivä.
examples.translation: I've had a really hard day.

examples.native: Sinulla ei ole mitään sanottavaa siitä, vai?
examples.translation: You don't have anything to say about it, do you?
I have a new job.

rules.title: Ablative source
rules.explanation: Ablative -lta/-ltä commonly expresses movement away from a surface or a source/person. Contrast it with allative destination and adessive location.

examples.translation: The islanders are asking us for help.
Tom was going to ask you about that.

examples.native: Kaikki kysyvät minulta millaista on olla värisokea.
examples.translation: Everyone asks me what it's like to be colour-blind.

rules.title: Conditional forms
rules.explanation: The conditional often contains -isi- and can mark hypothetical or polite meanings. Person endings still matter. Pitäisi commonly expresses should/ought in a construction that may require genitive marking.

examples.translation: Tom would've won easily.

examples.native: Hänen olisi pitänyt pitää suunsa kiinni.
examples.translation: She should have kept her mouth shut.

examples.native: Tom haluaa kysyä mitä Mari on puuhastellut, mutta hän tietää ettei hänen pitäisi.
examples.translation: Tom wants to ask what Mary has been doing, but he knows that he shouldn't.

rules.title: Questions and question particle
rules.explanation: Question words inflect for the needed case. The clitic -ko/-kö can turn a focused word into a yes/no question. It follows vowel harmony and can attach to more than verbs.

examples.translation: What happened before that?

examples.native: Meidän täytyy kertoa kaikille mitä tapahtui.
examples.translation: We have to tell everybody what happened.
Does a cow have a pink udder?

rules.title: Relative forms
rules.explanation: Joka forms relative clauses and inflects according to its role inside the clause. The antecedent helps choose number, but the relative clause supplies the case relation.

examples.translation: I travel almost every day.

examples.native: Voi olla, että se ei ollut Tomi, joka rikkoi ikkunan.
examples.translation: Tom might not be the one who broke the window.

examples.native: Te olette ainoita, jotka voivat auttaa minua.
examples.translation: You're the only one who can help me.

rules.title: Complement and condition
rules.explanation: Että introduces a content clause; jos a condition; kun a temporal clause; koska a cause; vaikka a concession. Finnish does not copy German verb-final order merely because a clause is subordinate.

examples.native: Voisitko katsoa hetken muualle kun vaihdan vaatteeni?
examples.translation: Would you mind looking the other way for just a minute while I change my clothes?

examples.native: Olen pahoillani kun olen antanut sinun odottaa.
examples.translation: I'm sorry I've kept you waiting so long.

examples.native: Yllä oleva diagrammi kommutoi aina ja vain, kun f on isomorfismi.
examples.translation: The diagram above commutes if and only if f is an isomorphism.

rules.title: Postpositions
rules.explanation: Many postpositions follow a noun in a governed case, frequently genitive. Some corresponding prepositions take another case. Learn a relation word with its complement pattern.

examples.translation: Just help me with this baggage.
Did he go to Hangzhou with his dad?

examples.native: Ajattelin, että saattaisit olla yksinäinen, joten tulin kylään viinipullon kanssa.
examples.translation: I thought you might be lonely, so I came over with a bottle of wine.

rules.title: Quantity and numerals
rules.explanation: Many cardinal quantities greater than one take singular partitive of the counted noun. Paljon/vähän interact with countability and case. Do not simply put a plural nominative after every number.

examples.translation: Tom scored four goals.

examples.native: Tom osaa puhua vain vähän ranskaa.
examples.translation: Tom can speak only a little French.
I know how much you value your privacy.

rules.title: Perfect participles
rules.explanation: A perfect uses an olla form plus a past active participle, with number agreement in relevant forms. Negative past constructions also use a participle but differ in auxiliary pattern.

examples.native: Hän meni Kiinaan sotilaana eikä koskaan tullut takaisin.
examples.translation: He went to China as a soldier, never to come back.
Tom didn't have much of a choice.

examples.native: Tämä ei ollut halpa, eikö niin?
examples.translation: This wasn't cheap, was it?

rules.title: Comparison and stance
rules.explanation: Parempi is adjectival better; paremmin adverbial better. Kuitenkin marks nevertheless and siksi a consequence. Ehkä limits certainty. Compare the form’s actual role before choosing an English gloss.

examples.native: Ehkä hän on italialainen tai espanjalainen.
examples.translation: Maybe he is Italian or Spanish.

examples.native: Minä pidän enemmän kesästä kuin talvesta.
examples.translation: I like summer better than winter.
Would you care to come with us?

passages.native: Opiskelen uutta kieltä. Luen joka päivä lyhyen tekstin ja kuuntelen selkeitä esimerkkejä. Kirjoitan hyödyllisiä sanoja vihkoon. Kun teen virheen, tarkistan säännön ja yritän uudelleen. Tavoitteeni on ymmärtää ihmisiä ja ilmaista ajatukseni selkeästi.
passages.translation: I am learning a new language. Each day, I read a short text and listen to clear examples. I write useful words in a notebook. When I make a mistake, I check the rule and try again. My goal is to understand people and express my ideas clearly.

grammarTerms: Noun
A word naming a person, thing or idea: student, book, freedom.
Verb
A word describing an action or state: read, know, be.
Subject
The participant linked to the main verb’s subject pattern. In The student reads a book, the student is the subject.
Object
A participant selected by a verb. In The student reads a book, a book is the direct object.
Agreement
One word changes to match another, for example an adjective matching a noun’s gender and number.
Case
A noun/pronoun form marking its relationship in a sentence. Cases can mark subjects, objects, possession or relations usually expressed by English prepositions.
Gender
A grammatical noun class. It does not always describe the sex of a person or any physical property.
Tense
A verb system that relates a situation to a time, often past or non-past.
Aspect
How a situation is viewed: unfolding, completed, habitual, experienced or in a resulting state.
Infinitive
A non-finite verb form often used for a dictionary entry or a complement. It does not by itself give the ordinary person/tense pattern.
Participle
A verb-derived form used in compound predicates or as a modifier; its exact function depends on the language and construction.
Clause
A unit organised around a predicate. One sentence can contain several clauses.
Register
Language choices suited to a situation: casual conversation, polite requests, academic writing or another context.
